title: Damodaran Values Anthropic at $1.48 Trillion, Slams Founder Voting Control
excerpt: The NYU professor's base case sits at the low end of the IPO range — and he says the five-class structure, with founders holding 50.1% of votes, neutralises public shareholders.
body:
• NYU professor Aswath Damodaran values Anthropic's equity at about $1.475 trillion — the low end of the $1.5 trillion to $2 trillion IPO pricing range — in his valuation published after the October 26 S-1 filing.
  • His base case assumes revenue approaching $1 trillion by 2036, a 27.5% operating margin after regulatory drag, three dollars of revenue per dollar of reinvestment and a 9.74% cost of capital.
  • He attacked the governance structure: a single Class F share held by the founders carries 50.1% of voting power, while a Long-Term Benefit Trust elects a majority of the board — public shareholders, he wrote, are effectively neutralised.
  • For investors: Damodaran's range runs from negative equity in a worst case to $4.04 trillion in a best case — the IPO price, not the business, is the decision.

Aswath Damodaran has put a number on Anthropic, and a warning on its share structure. In a valuation published after Anthropic made its S-1 prospectus public on October 26, the New York University finance professor estimated the AI company's equity at $1.475 trillion, at the lower end of the $1.5 trillion to $2 trillion offer range, as reported by Stocktwits. His full workings are in his post, The Anthropic IPO Arrives.

The valuation

Damodaran's story for Anthropic is revenue approaching $1 trillion by 2036, from $16.3 billion in the first half of 2026 — itself up from $1.2 billion a year earlier. He models a target operating margin of 32.5%, trimmed to 27.5% for regulatory effects, reinvestment efficiency of three dollars of revenue per dollar of capital, a 9.74% cost of capital and a 10% probability of failure. His scenario range is wide: best-case 2036 revenue of $1.5 trillion, worst-case $200 billion, and an equity value range from negative in the worst case to $4.04 trillion in the best. Expenses growing more slowly than revenue put the company, in his reading, on a path to significant profitability — but he described the prospectus as long and filled with distractions, comparing valuing Anthropic to reviewing a kindergartner's report card to decide a college fund.

"I think Anthropic has managed to put those companies to shame with its combination of a benefit corporation structure (which gives the company the legal license to do pretty much whatever it wants with your money) and a voting share design that is so deviously self-serving that it would put Kim Jong Un to shame."

— Aswath Damodaran, NYU Stern

The governance problem

The structure Damodaran criticised has five share classes. Public investors buy Class A shares with standard voting rights. A single non-economic Class F share, held by a Founder LLC comprising Anthropic's seven co-founders, carries 50.1% of the voting power on matters put to shareholders, no matter how many more shares are issued. A separate Class T share held by the Long-Term Benefit Trust lets the trust elect and remove the directors who form a majority of the board. Strategic investors such as Amazon and Google hold non-voting Class N shares. Anthropic is also a public benefit corporation, and its prospectus states it may make decisions that balance shareholder interests against its company purpose even when those decisions hurt the share price. Damodaran, who holds dual-class shares in Alphabet and Meta and said he draws no absolute line against founder control, argued this combination goes further than either: it does not protect society from AI's risks, he wrote, but concentrates power in the founders and the trustees they selected.

The numbers underneath

The filing shows why both the valuation and the argument are live. Anthropic spent nearly $9 billion on computing in the first half of 2026 and has committed to at least $110 billion of spending with Amazon through April 2036 and at least $114.5 billion with Google through July 2033. More than 1,900 customers generated at least $1 million each in trailing annual revenue by September 30, and more than 11,900 generated at least $100,000, up from 950 a year earlier — but two unnamed customers accounted for about 23% of first-half revenue. A Public Benefit Fund already holds about 5% of fully diluted shares in non-voting stock, and the board may issue up to a further 2% each time the share price rises 50% above the previous milestone, a dilution mechanism public investors cannot vote down.

What it means for buyers

Damodaran's conclusion is procedural, not a buy or sell call: at a price well above $1.475 trillion, investors are paying for a story better than his upbeat base case, with governance rights that cannot correct course if the story disappoints. He said he will sit out if the IPO prices well above his value. The offering, expected next month, would test whether public markets accept founder control of this degree at a valuation above SpaceX's $1.77 trillion listing record. For retail investors, the practical point is in the prospectus itself: Class A holders generally cannot affect the outcome of any shareholder matter, and there is no time-based sunset on the founder share — it fades only when fewer than three founders remain, followed by a 450-day transition.
